(CNN) -- Canadian ski resort gondola cars that were left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers inside failed because ice buildup snapped a supporting tower, the resort said Thursday. One gondola car is suspended above an icy creek at a ski resort near Whistler, British Columbia. In a rare occurrence called ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and turned to ice Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a press release Thursday. The lift hangs from a tower that is spliced into two parts. Extremely cold temperatures caused the ice buildup that exerted 800 tons of pressure between the two parts that hold the tower together, causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb. The section of the lift affected by the accident had 15 cars going up the mountain and 15 coming down at the time, but they weren't carrying a lot of passengers, according to Doug Forseth, senior vice president of the resort. He said 53 passengers had been rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured. "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident. They are trying to figure out what caused the water to pool. He said independent structural engineers are examining the tower from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said. At least two gondola cars broke away and hit the ground, both from relatively low heights near the tower that split, and caused the system's heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble said Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car." The broken Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers checked eight similar towers across the two mountains of the resort. All passed those inspections, and are open Thursday, the release said. The British Columbia Authority says it does not expect to rescind operating permits on any lifts at the resort, other than the Excaliber Gondola. Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort was similarly damaged by ice in December 2006. The damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, so no one was endangered, he said. The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort's business was not significantly disrupted. "We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Holes have been drilled in the bases of towers so that water can drain out, Colburn said. CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Officials at a Canadian ski resort said Thursday that a buildup of ice caused a gondola support tower to break, leaving cars hanging and rocking in the air with frightened skiers trapped inside.

One of the gondola cabins was left suspended over a frozen creek at a resort near Whistler, British Columbia.

According to a Thursday news release from a resort official, the incident happened Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb, about 177 kilometers, or 110 miles, north of Vancouver. The resort said water had entered the bottom portion of a lift tower and frozen there, a rare phenomenon known as “ice-jacking.”

The lift tower is made of two joined sections. Whistler Blackcomb said extremely low temperatures led to ice expansion that created about 800 tons of pressure between the two connected parts, eventually forcing them apart and causing the rupture.

Doug Forseth, the resort’s senior vice president, said that when the accident occurred, 15 gondola cars were traveling uphill and another 15 were heading downhill on the affected part of the lift. However, he said the cars were not heavily occupied. Forseth said rescuers removed 53 people from the stranded cabins.

No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort suffered serious injuries.

“This failure is a very unusual situation because towers are not typically built in a way that would permit water to get inside,” said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering company that examined the accident.

Sparks said investigators are still working to determine why water accumulated inside the tower. He also said independent structural engineers from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers are inspecting it.

“The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period,” Sparks said.

At least two gondola cabins detached and fell to the ground from relatively low elevations close to the broken tower, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter with CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. Their fall caused the system’s heavy cable to lose tension.

“One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house,” Noble said Wednesday. “Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car.”

The damaged Excaliber Gondola remained closed Thursday.

Whistler engineers inspected eight comparable towers on the resort’s two mountains. The resort said in its release that all of them passed inspection and were operating Thursday.

The British Columbia Safety Authority said it did not expect to revoke operating permits for any resort lifts except the Excaliber Gondola.

Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said one of his resort’s lift towers sustained similar ice-related damage in December 2006. In that case, the problem was found in the morning before the ski area opened, so no one was put at risk.

Colburn said the damaged tower was replaced in roughly three weeks, and the resort’s operations were not seriously affected.

“We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don’t have any water in them, and we’ve worked with the manufacturers,” he said.

Colburn said holes have been drilled into the bottoms of the towers to allow water to drain.

CNN’s Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

**BREAKING NEWS REPORT — WHISTLER, British Columbia**  
**Gondola cabins left dangling after lift failure at major Canadian ski resort; investigators cite ice-related tower rupture**

A dramatic gondola failure at **Whistler Blackcomb**, one of Canada’s busiest ski resorts, left several cabins hanging at steep angles and forced dozens of passengers to be rescued from the air after a lift tower partially collapsed near Whistler Village.

Authorities and engineers later determined the incident was caused by **water that had entered a hollow steel lift tower and frozen**, expanding with enough force to split and deform the tower — a phenomenon commonly referred to as **“ice jacking.”**

## What happened

The failure occurred on the **Excalibur Gondola**, a key lift connecting Whistler Village with Blackcomb Mountain. A support tower near the lower section of the lift suffered a structural failure, causing the haul rope to sag and several gondola cabins to drop or tilt sharply.

Witnesses described cabins suddenly lurching, dropping, and coming to rest at abnormal angles. Some cabins were left suspended above roadways and resort infrastructure, while others came close to the ground. The scene prompted an immediate emergency response from fire crews, ski patrol, police, ambulance personnel, and lift maintenance teams.

## Passengers rescued from suspended cabins

Roughly **50-plus passengers** were on the affected section of the gondola at the time. Rescue crews evacuated riders cabin by cabin using a mix of:

- **Aerial ladders**
- **Rope-rescue systems**
- **Harnesses and belay lines**
- **Ground-based access where cabins had dropped low enough**

Crews prioritized passengers in cabins that were most steeply angled or closest to hazards. Some riders were lowered by rope; others were helped down by ladder where the cabin position allowed.

There were **no fatalities**, though a number of passengers suffered injuries, most described as minor to moderate, including bruises, strains, and shock-related symptoms. Several people were assessed by paramedics, and some were taken to hospital for further evaluation.

## Engineering findings: water, freezing, and tower deformation

The central engineering finding was that the tower did not fail because of normal operating loads alone. Investigators found that **water had accumulated inside the hollow steel tower structure**. When temperatures dropped, the trapped water froze and expanded.

That expansion exerted enormous pressure from inside the tower, eventually causing the steel to deform and split. Once the tower’s geometry changed, it could no longer properly support the gondola’s rope system, leading to the sudden sagging and displacement of cabins.

Key findings included:

- The affected tower was a **hollow steel structure**.
- Water had entered or accumulated inside the tower.
- Freezing temperatures caused the water to expand.
- The internal pressure ruptured or distorted the tower.
- The resulting deformation compromised the rope alignment and tower support system.

Investigators described the mechanism as unusual but mechanically explainable: water expansion during freezing can generate forces strong enough to damage steel if it is trapped in a confined space.

## Resort and lift response

Whistler Blackcomb shut down the Excalibur Gondola immediately after the incident and launched a full technical review with lift engineers, the lift manufacturer, and provincial safety authorities.

The damaged tower was removed or repaired, affected components were examined, and the gondola did not return to service until regulators and engineers were satisfied it could operate safely.

The resort also moved to inspect other lift towers and related infrastructure to determine whether similar water intrusion or freeze damage could be present elsewhere.

## Safety inspections ordered

Following the incident, safety officials required broader inspections of comparable lift structures, especially hollow towers where water intrusion could create the same freeze-expansion hazard.

Inspection measures included:

- Checking lift towers for **cracks, bulging, deformation, or splitting**
- Looking for evidence of **water accumulation**
- Verifying **drainage pathways**
- Inspecting welds, caps, seams, and tower bases
- Reviewing maintenance and inspection records
- Assessing whether design changes or added drainage were needed

Operators across the region were advised to ensure hollow lift towers could not trap water in ways that would allow ice pressure to build unseen.

## Broader safety implications

The Whistler incident became a significant case study in cold-weather lift engineering. It highlighted that ski-lift safety is not only about cables, brakes, motors, and evacuation systems, but also about hidden structural risks inside tower components.

The main safety lessons were:

1. **Water intrusion must be treated as a structural hazard in freezing climates.**  
2. **Hollow steel towers need reliable drainage and inspection access.**  
3. **Visual inspections alone may miss internal freeze damage until deformation appears.**  
4. **Emergency evacuation planning is essential for gondola systems operating over roads, buildings, or difficult terrain.**

## Current status

The Excalibur Gondola was repaired and returned to service after engineering work and regulatory approval. The incident did not result in fatalities, but it remains one of the more serious lift failures in Canadian ski-resort history and led to heightened scrutiny of gondola tower inspection practices in cold environments.

**WHISTLER, British Columbia —** Gondola cabins carrying skiers and snowboarders plunged toward the ground or were left dangling in midair after a lift tower split apart at Whistler Blackcomb, forcing a major rescue operation and prompting an engineering investigation into the rare structural failure.

Resort officials said a steel support tower failed after it cracked and separated, causing the haul rope to drop and several gondola cars to lurch violently. Some cabins struck the ground or nearby structures, while others hung at steep angles above the village area.

Engineering investigators later focused on what officials described as “ice jacking” inside the tower. Water had entered the hollow steel structure, froze and expanded, splitting the tower from within.

An engineering official familiar with the investigation said the failure was consistent with internal ice pressure. “When water gets trapped inside a confined steel member and freezes, the expansion can generate tremendous force,” the official said. “In this case, that force was enough to rupture the tower.”

Resort officials said the lift had undergone routine inspections before the accident and that there had been no obvious indication the tower was in danger of failing. The Excalibur Gondola, built by Doppelmayr, was part of one of North America’s busiest ski-area lift networks.

“We will not operate this lift again until we are satisfied it is safe,” the resort said, adding that it was cooperating with engineers, the lift manufacturer and provincial regulators.

The accident disrupted operations at the resort, though other lifts continued running. Whistler Blackcomb said it would review inspection procedures and maintenance protocols in light of the findings.

Lift-safety specialists said the incident was highly unusual. Modern gondola towers are designed with significant safety margins, and catastrophic tower failures are rare. But investigators said the split tower showed how trapped water, freezing temperatures and hidden corrosion or drainage problems can create hazards not visible during ordinary external checks.

“This type of failure is not something passengers or lift operators would necessarily see developing from the outside,” the engineering official said. “That is why drainage, sealing and internal inspection details are critical in cold-weather structures.”
